title: Weldability and welding technology of oxide dispersion-strengthened (ODS) superalloys: a review
abstract: Abstract Oxide dispersion strengthened (ODS) superalloys are a type of high-performance material that uses nanoscale oxide particles (such as Y 2 O 3  and Al 2 O 3 ) as strengthening phases. Due to their excellent high-temperature strength and radiation resistance, they have important application prospects in aerospace, nuclear energy, and other fields. However, the agglomeration and decomposition of oxide particles, the formation of porosity defects, and high residual stress during the welding process limit its engineering applications. This article systematically reviews the research progress of ODS superalloy welding. Introduced the alloy system and the mechanisms of dispersion strengthening and grain refinement strengthening. The three major challenges in the welding process were analyzed in detail: the evolution of oxide particles, porosity defects, and long-term performance degradation. Based on this, the article discusses strategies to improve welding quality. Optimization of process parameters requires a balance between defect control and retention of oxide particles; Composition design can regulate the content of key elements to improve the thermal stability of particles, but it also comes with a loss of some performance; Post-weld treatment faces a fundamental contradiction between stress relief and particle stability. Future research directions such as AI-assisted process optimization and in-situ characterization technology were proposed to provide reference for promoting the development of ODS superalloy welding technology.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Oxide Dispersed Strengthened (ODS) superalloys are an important branch of superalloys [ 1 ]. It is a kind of material made by uniformly dispersing nano-oxide dispersion-strengthened particles (hereinafter abbreviated as "oxide particles") into a superalloy matrix by hot extrusion [ 2 ,  3 ] and hot isostatic pressing [ 4 ,  5 – 6 ]. Traditional superalloys can improve the strength of materials by precipitation strengthening and solution strengthening [ 1 ] so that the materials can serve for a long time at a certain stress and in the range of about 760–1100 ℃. However, when the service temperature exceeds 1100 ℃, the main strengthening phase [Ni 3 (Al, Ti)] will coarsen and dissolve, which significantly reduces the properties of the material. In the 1960s, International Nickel Company first used ThO 2  as a dispersion strengthening phase and developed TD-Ni alloy, which marked that ODS superalloy moved from theory to reality and was an innovation of the material strengthening mechanism in a high-temperature environment. In the early 1970s, the company used the mechanical alloying (MA) process to uniformly distribute Y 2 O 3  oxide particles in the alloy, which promoted the rapid development of ODS superalloy. Nowadays, ODS superalloys not only have basic nickel-based alloys but also extend to iron-based and cobalt-based alloys. The strengthening mechanism mainly includes dispersion strengthening and fine grain strengthening. By adding the second phase to hinder dislocation movement and Zener pinning grain boundary of the second-phase particles [ 7 ,  8 – 9 ], the material has excellent high-temperature mechanical properties, such as oxidation, heat corrosion resistance, and fracture toughness. It can be widely used in aerospace, energy, and other industries to meet the material requirements in extremely high temperature and pressure environments [ 10 ,  11 ].

However, the ODS superalloy welding technique comes with challenges. Defects include porosity and cracks that are easily produced during the welding process [ 12 ,  13 ], and the oxide particles frequently agglomerate or decompose [ 14 ,  15 ], resulting in a loss of strength in the welded joint. Therefore, the widespread practical application of ODS superalloys depends on solving welding defects and studying the evolution process of oxide particles during welding. Researchers have continued to focus on ODS superalloys in recent years. Figure  1  shows the research trend of retrieving "superalloy," "ODS," and "welding" and retrieving the "ODS" and "welding" keywords in EI and the number of articles published in the recent 20 years. The retrieval scope includes journal articles, conference articles, conference proceedings, dissertations, and standards. The development of oxide particles, porosity, and degradation of long-term service behaviors' difficulties during the welding of ODS superalloy is reviewed in this article. Furthermore, it reviews how welding techniques such as friction stir welding (FSW), laser welding, and TIG welding, as well as process parameter adjustments, material composition modifications, and post-weld treatment, affect weld defects. The purpose of this review is to provide a guide for future acquisitions of better ODS superalloy welded joints. Fig. 1 Trend chart of research publications on ODS superalloy welding

sections.heading: ODS superalloy design principles and strengthening mechanism
ODS superalloy composition design
paragraphs: Depending on the main component, ODS superalloys can be divided into nickel-based and iron-based superalloys. The most common ODS superalloys are the ones composed of nickel, such as MA754 [ 15 ] and MA6000 [ 16 ]. Based on chromium quantity, iron-based ODS superalloys are further divided as low-activation ferritic steels and low-activation ferritic/martensitic dual-phase steels, such as MA957 [ 17 ], 14YWT [ 18 ], and ODS-Eurofer [ 19 ]. Iron-based ODS superalloys are cheaper and simpler to manufacture than nickel-based ODS superalloys, but they have poorer mechanical properties at higher temperatures.

For the purpose of enhancing the material's mechanical properties, ODS superalloys use uniformly distributed oxide particles as the strengthening phase. The additional oxide particles include Y 2 O 3 , Al 2 O 3 , La 2 O 3 , and Cr 2 O 3 . The most prevalent of these particles are Y 2 O 3  and Al 2 O 3 , which have high melting points (2410 °C and 2050 °C, respectively) and stable structures at high temperatures, making them appropriate for high-temperature applications [ 20 ]. The impacts of oxide particles Y 2 O 3  and Al 2 O 3  strengthening particles on the mechanical properties of NiCr substrates were compared by Srinivasan et al. [ 21 ], who found that the two types of particles contribute to the material's strength in distinct ways (as shown in Fig.  2 ). Hall–Petch strengthening and Zener pinning are the main strengthening mechanisms of Y 2 O 3  particles ( σ HP :  σ Orowan  = 2:1), while Hall–Petch strengthening is the primary strengthening mechanism of Al 2 O 3  particles ( σ HP :  σ Orowan  = 5:1). According to Peng et al. [ 22 ], the interplanar spacing of {200}Ni and {600}Y 2 O 3  was 0.1762 nm and 0.1767 nm, respectively; {220}Ni and {653}Y 2 O 3  were 0.1246 nm and 0.1267 nm, respectively; and {210}Ni and {611}Y 2 O 3  were 0.1576 nm and 0.1598 nm, respectively. The extremely small mismatch shows that the Y 2 O 3  particles and matrix can form a cohesive interaction. Consequently, the main strengthening phase of ODS superalloys is now the oxide particle Y 2 O 3  owing to its lattice compatibility and high-temperature stability. Fig. 2 Variation of  a  grain size,  b  particle size,   c ,  d  hardness with time at 1373 K. Reprinted from [ 21 ] with permission. Copyright 2006 Elsevier

sections.heading: Dispersion strengthening
paragraphs: The primary strengthening mechanism in ODS superalloys is dispersion strengthening, in which oxide particles hinder dislocation motion via the Orowan mechanism. When dislocations bypass these particles, they leave behind dislocation loops, thereby enhancing the strength. This strengthening contribution can be approximated as ∆ τ  ∝  f ^(1/2)/ r , where the strengthening increment increases with the particle volume fraction  f  and decreases with the particle radius  r . Yao et al. [ 23 ] studied the strengthening mechanism of Y-Zr-O oxide dispersion-strengthened molybdenum alloy and found that the yield strength, microhardness, and elongation of the material were improved to some extent after adding Y-Zr-O particles. This is due to the formation, obstruction, and accumulation of dislocations in the preparation process of sized Y-Zr-O particles, thus improving the strength of materials. As shown in Fig.  3 , the author also obtained the contribution of different strengthening mechanisms to material strength through theoretical calculation and thought that the main strengthening mechanisms were dispersion strengthening and fine grain strengthening. Rajulapati et al. [ 24 ] studied the effect of Y 2 O 3  content on the strengthening mechanism of 9-Cr ODS steel. It is found that at room temperature and high temperature (700 ℃), dislocation and the Orowan strengthening mechanism contribute more to the yield strength of materials. However, at higher temperatures, the dispersion strengthening effect weakens. Fig. 3 The calculated yield strength of various strengthening effects and experimental value of pure Mo, Mo-1Y 2 O 3 -0.6Zr, and Mo-1Y 2 O 3 -1.2Zr alloys. Reprinted from [ 23 ] with permission. Copyright 2022 Elsevier

sections.heading: Grain refinement strengthening
paragraphs: Another strengthening mechanism in ODS superalloys is fine grain strengthening. The Zener pinning effect of oxide particles pins grain boundaries, effectively suppressing grain boundary migration and hindering grain growth. Meanwhile, in certain alloy systems, oxide particles can also serve as heterogeneous nucleation sites to promote nucleation and indirectly refine grain size. Fine-grain strengthening can be described by the Hall–Petch relationship, where finer grains lead to higher yield strength. The impact of different particle parameters on Zener pinning and the regulation of grain size distribution, as visualized using phase-field modeling, was demonstrated by Manna et al. [ 25 ] (as shown in Fig.  4 ). The pinning effect has been demonstrated to be more significant the bigger the volume fraction of the additional particles and the smaller the size. In the meantime, grain dimensions and shape are also influenced by particle mobility, growth direction, and energy ratio, limiting grain coarsening. Fig. 4 Phase-field simulations of the effect of different factors on particle alignment for Zener pinning:  a  small size and large volume fraction;  b  high aspect ratio and small volume fraction;  c  small size, low grain boundary energy, and small volume fraction;  d  small size, high mobility, and small volume fraction;  e  large size and small volume fraction;  f  small size and small volume fraction. Reprinted from [ 25 ] wtih permission. Copyright 2023 Elsevier

Before and after FSW of ODS superalloy PM2000 following recrystallization treatment, Chen et al. [ 26 ] noted the alterations in oxide particles. The findings demonstrated that the base material region's oxide particles were positioned along the boundaries. Following recrystallization, the oxide particles tended to impede grain boundary motion, displaying a pinning effect (as shown in Fig.  5 ). Some literature has mentioned similar conclusions [ 27 ,  28 ]. Fig. 5 TEM micrographs of the base metal area:  a, b  before,  c, d  after the recrystallization  treatment.  Reprinted from [ 26 ] with permission. Copyright 2010 Elsevier

ODS Inconel 625 was tested with directed energy deposition (DED) technology by Zou et al. [ 29 ]. Grain refinement can be achieved in ODS superalloys by incorporating 2.5 wt% La 2 O 3  oxide particles into the original Inconel 625 alloy. It was discovered that when La 2 O 3  particles were added, La 2 Ti 2 O 7  particles precipitated, and the grain size dropped from 433 ± 190 to 314 ± 200 μm. The yield strength of Inconel 625 was 401 ± 5 MPa, the ultimate tensile strength was 635 ± 10 MPa, and the total elongation was 55%, as shown by an analysis of the stress–strain curve of the prepared ODS Inconel 625 walls (as shown in Fig.  6 ). Inconel 625-La 2 O 3 's yield strength was 412 ± 6 MPa, its ultimate tensile strength was 672 ± 13 MPa, and its total elongation was 52%, suggesting that the material's strength had somewhat increased. The impact of Y 2 O 3  on the mechanical properties of weld joints was studied by Zhang et al. [ 30 ]. They discovered that adding oxide particles enhanced the amount of acicular ferrite, prevented the formation of martensite and bainite, effectively refined the grain structure, greatly enhanced the material's mechanical properties, and produced a tensile strength of 769 MPa. Fig. 6 Engineering stress–strain curves of IN625 and IN625-La 2 O 3  samples. Reprinted from [ 29 ] with permission. Copyright 2024 Elsevier

However, during welding, thermal cycling in the heat-affected zone (HAZ) and fusion zone (FZ) can lead to the agglomeration or decomposition of oxide particles, thereby weakening the Zener pinning effect and inducing grain growth. This oxide particle evolution reduces the number of effective obstacles for dislocation motion (Orowan strengthening), while grain coarsening decreases yield strength via the Hall–Petch relationship. Consequently, softened regions may develop in the welded joint of ODS superalloys, compromising its reliability. The evolution of oxide particles during welding is discussed in detail in Sect.  3.1 .

sections.heading: The challenges of welding ODS superalloys
paragraphs: Laser welding, TIG welding, and FSW are common welding techniques for ODS superalloys. Conventional fusion welding often results in the loss of oxide particles because internal oxide particles are sensitive to changes at high welding temperatures. As a result, low-temperature FSW has been the focus of major ODS superalloy welding research. The weld microstructure and mechanical properties of typical alloy steels are greatly influenced by variables such as fluid motion [ 31 ,  32 – 33 ], transient temperature gradients [ 34 ,  35 – 36 ], and melt pool solidification rates [ 37 ,  38 – 39 ]. For the ODS superalloys, the physicochemical properties are further changed by the inclusion of oxide particles. As a result, the primary challenges during welding are mechanical properties and weld quality decline brought on by the oxide particle evolution.

sections.heading: Agglomeration of oxide particles
paragraphs: Significant oxide particle agglomeration was noted by Dawson et al. [ 40 ] during FSW of MA956 (as shown in Fig.  7 ). The findings showed that a more noticeable increase in particle size was caused by raising the tool rotation speed and lowering the transverse travel speed. This is explained by the tendency of larger heat input to decompose oxide particles, which increases churning. However, the majority of oxide particles in the weld stirred zone are preserved because of the low decomposition level of oxide particles and the low welding temperature of FSW, which increases the quantity of agglomeration oxide particles. During TIG welding of MGH956 superalloy, Zhu et al. [ 41 ] noticed the agglomeration of oxide particles along the pore walls of several gas pores within the weld (as shown in Fig.  8 ). The agglomeration particles are composed of Al, Ti, Y, and O by EDS analysis. It can be determined that the formation of pores is related to the added oxide particles. Usually, small particles have higher surface energy in a molten pool. In order to reduce the free energy of the whole system, small particles tend to agglomerate spontaneously. During the welding process, oxide particles are easy to adsorb gas, and with the agglomeration of oxide particles, pores that are difficult to escape are formed. Therefore, it can also explain the agglomeration of oxide particles on the inner wall of weld porosity. Getto et al. [ 42 ] used friction stir welding to join MA956. Using a HAADF image, they found that the average diameter of oxide particles was 10.6 nm in base metal (BM), 18.4 nm in medium heat input (SM-M: 300 rpm + 50 mmpm), and 19.7 nm in high heat input (SM-H: 500 rpm + 25 mmpm). With the increase of heat input, the average diameter of oxide particles increases significantly, which proves the particles' agglomeration during welding. Fig. 7 TEM images illustrating  a ,  b  the agglomeration of oxide particles in two  different regions. Reprinted from [ 40 ] with permission. Copyright 2017 Elsevier Fig. 8 SEM image of TIG-welded joint. Reprinted from [ 41 ] with permission. Copyright 2014 Elsevier

sections.heading: Oxide particle agglomeration in post-welding service environment
paragraphs: Getto et al. [ 42 ] also studied the phenomenon of oxide particle agglomeration under non-thermal drive and irradiated the MA956 weld with 5 MeV Fe ions at a dose of 50–200 dpa in the range of 400–500 °C. Some results are shown in Fig.  9 . Ion irradiation has the least effect on the particle size of the base metal, and there are diameter peaks at similar positions regardless of irradiation temperature. However, ion irradiation has a great influence on the weld, and the average diameter distribution of oxide particles under SM-M and SM-H conditions after irradiation is smoother than that of the base metal. And at 450–500 ℃, the peak diameter shifts to the right, and the oxide particles appear obviously coarsening. It is suggested that the competitive mechanism of radiation-enhanced diffusion and Ostwald coarsening is at 400 ℃ and 450 ℃, and Ostwald coarsening is dominant at 500 ℃. Therefore, oxide particles in ODS superalloy are not only easy to agglomerate during welding but also move and agglomerate under "non-thermal" conditions. Fig. 9 Diameter distribution for dispersoids measured via HAADF imaging at 100 dpa for  a  BM,  b  SZ-M, and  c  SZ-H. Reprinted from [ 42 ] with permission. Copyright 2022 Elsevier

sections.heading: Decomposition of oxide particles
paragraphs: Oxide particles may melt and decompose during the fusion welding process because of the comparatively high temperatures involved. The evolution of Y 2 O 3  particle decomposition in ODS superalloys was methodically explained by Kenel et al. [ 43 ], who summarized three modes of transformation for oxide particles: first, they react with superalloy elements to form slag, which floats to the top of the molten pool; second, they disperse uniformly within the alloy, greatly reducing grain size; and third, they break down into nanoscale metallic compounds or segregate at grain boundaries. Near the grain boundaries of the iron-based ODS superalloy DYAL, Kehagias et al. [ 44 ] found oxide dispersion particle-depleted zones that are prone to occur under heat treatment and high-temperature deformation. This region is parallel to the alloy matrix's twinning region (as shown in Fig.  10 ). The phenomenon could be explained by incomplete mechanical alloying of the base material and localized diffusion and rearrangement of matrix elements due to the enhanced stress field brought on by high temperatures. Increased stress fields at high temperatures, which result in localized matrix element diffusion and rearrangement, and insufficient mechanical alloying of the base material are two possible explanations of this condition. Similar observations of oxide particle melting and decomposition during FSW of MA956 have been reported by Dawson et al. [ 40 ] They pointed out, nonetheless, that the phenomenon was only seen in welds with high-temperature input (as shown in Fig.  11 ). Fig. 10 An oxide-depleted zone. Reprinted from [ 44 ] with permission. Copyright 1969  Nature Fig. 11 TEM images showing examples of oxide particle decomposition. Reprinted from [ 40 ] with permission. Copyright 2017 Elsevier

In summary, the instability of oxide particles is the main challenge for the widespread application of ODS superalloy welded parts. During the welding process, oxide particles in the molten pool tend to agglomerate due to energy-driven reduction of the system energy. Therefore, the agglomeration behavior of oxide particles can be observed at grain boundaries [ 15 ], pore walls [ 41 ], and fusion lines [ 45 ]. Particles on the inner wall of pores increase the mass of pores in the molten pool, and particle agglomeration at grain boundaries and fusion lines will block the gas escape channel, which will lead to serious pores in welds and increase the brittleness of materials. For the high-temperature fusion welding, the oxide particles are easy to decompose during the welding process (Y 2 O 3  → 2[Y] + 3[O]). On the one hand, the oxide particles react with the base metal elements to form an impurity phase ( x [Y] +  y [Al] +  z [O] → Y x Al y O z ,  x [Y] +  y [Ti] +  z [O] → Y x Ti y O z ); on the other hand, the dispersion strengthening mechanism and Zener pinning mechanism of ODS superalloy disappear, and the mechanical properties of ODS superalloy are greatly reduced. Compared with fusion welding, friction stir welding is accompanied by strong stirring and extrusion of the stirring head, and the tiny pores in the weld may be closed, which can effectively reduce the porosity of the weld. At the same time, the welding temperature of friction stir welding is lower than the melting point of oxide particles, and the dispersion strengthening phase [ 46 ] is retained after welding, which stabilizes the mechanical properties of the material. However, under some conditions (such as ion irradiation), the long-term service of the weld will also lead to the agglomeration of oxide particles. Therefore, controlling the agglomeration and decomposition of oxide particles and reducing the changed oxide particles are the important research directions of ODS superalloy welding in the future.

sections.heading: Inherent porosity susceptibility
paragraphs: Due to the unique material composition of ODS superalloys, they exhibit a high susceptibility to porosity. Grain boundaries normally serve as routes for gas release; however, their migration and growth are inhibited by the Zener pinning effect of oxide particles. This restricted grain boundary movement impedes the removal of gases, causing them to remain in the alloy and eventually develop into pores. In ODS superalloys, the pores typically exhibit an ellipsoidal morphology due to the agglomeration of oxide particles [ 41 ,  47 ]. Fu et al. [ 48 ] studied the microstructure of pulsed laser welded joints in ODS alloy. They observed large pores at the weld bottom and incomplete penetration in 1 mm thick plates with a pulse duration of 2–2.5 ms. When the pulse duration exceeded 2.5 ms, complete penetration was achieved but accompanied by material loss, and micro-voids were present in the weld (as shown in Fig.  12 ). As pulse duration increased, welding stability improved and large pores decreased due to the longer time available for gas escape. Huai et al. [ 49 ] investigated the weldability of MGH956 using argon arc welding (AAW) and electron beam welding (EBW). The EBW joints exhibited better room-temperature plasticity and comparatively lower porosity than the AAW joints (as shown in Fig.  13 ). This is attributed to two factors: first, the argon shielding gas used in AAW can become trapped in the weld; second, the prolonged molten pool duration and slow cooling rate hinder the buoyancy-driven escape of accumulated internal gases. In contrast, EBW is performed in a high vacuum environment, eliminating the risk of residual shielding gas in the molten pool. However, porosity cannot be completely eliminated even under vacuum conditions. Zhu et al. [ 41 ] found that when using TIG welding to weld ODS superalloy MGH956, a large number of pores appeared in the weld area, with pore sizes ranging from a few micrometers to several tens of micrometers (as shown in Fig.  13 ). And explain the reasons for the formation of pores, which are related to the adsorption of oxide particles and the manufacturing process of the alloy. In summary, the pinning effect of oxide particles not only inhibits molten pool flow during welding but also hinders the coalescence and escape of pores, thereby promoting the formation of internal porosity in ODS superalloys. Fig. 12 Weld bead morphology at a power of 2500 W and pulse durations of  a  2 ms,  b  2.5 ms,  c  3 ms,  d  3.5 ms, and  e  4 ms. Reprinted from [ 48 ] under the Creative Commons CC BY 4.0 license Fig. 13 Pore distribution of TIG  welding joints. Reprinted from [ 41 ] with permission. Copyright 2014 Elsevier

sections.heading: Effect of melt flow behavior on porosity formation
paragraphs: The inherent characteristics of ODS superalloys dictate that welding pores are inherently difficult to escape; however, their final distribution and quantity are equally dependent on the fluid dynamics of the molten pool prior to solidification. Within the pool, the liquid metal forms a complex flow field under the influence of multiple driving forces, thereby affecting the migration paths and final positions of the pores. Han et al. [ 50 ] clarified the differences in the dominant driving forces for three distinct welding processes through three-dimensional numerical simulations. In GTA welding, the molten pool flow is dominated by Marangoni convection, a flow driven by surface tension gradients that transports liquid metal from the pool center to its edges. This mechanism carries gas to the fusion line, which explains the phenomenon of pores being distributed in chains along the fusion line in ODS alloy welds. In laser welding, however, recoil pressure takes over as the dominant driving force. As this force acts opposite to the direction of gas escape, compounded by the increased melt viscosity from the pinning effect imparted by oxide particles in ODS superalloys, making gas escape even more difficult. In laser-GTA hybrid welding, recoil pressure remains the dominant force and differs only in that the molten pool is wider due to the additional heat source, which provides more favorable conditions for gas escape. Further evidence from Wang et al. [ 51 ] in laser powder bed fusion (LB-PBF) research shows that as heat input increases, the content of Y-Al-O oxide inclusions in ODS-FeCrAl steel decreases from 0.8% to less than 0.1%. These less-dense oxides float to the surface after multiple remelting cycles and are transported to the sides of the molten pool by Marangoni convection. This mechanism validates the role of Marangoni convection in transporting secondary phases, providing experimental evidence for the aforementioned explanation of chain-like pore distribution. Research by Cho et al. [ 52 ] on the GMAW molten pool indicates that material transport is dominated by droplet impingement and is entirely dependent on convection, with diffusion being negligible. This implies that welding pores, as a "secondary phase," are likewise dominated by convection. Consequently, intense droplet impingement could potentially entrain bubbles into the depth of the molten pool, thereby increasing porosity susceptibility.

The porosity behavior of ODS superalloy is affected by its intrinsic material properties and molten pool hydrodynamics. Generally speaking, the porosity problem is more obvious in fusion welding than in solid-state welding. Oxide particles in ODS superalloy play a pinning role. This effect limits grain boundary movement, increases melt viscosity, and hinders gas escape. The distribution and number of pores are determined by the dominant driving force of different fusion welding methods. In GTA welding, Marangoni convection transports gas to the fusion line, resulting in chain pore distribution. This convection also transports gases, which might otherwise rise vertically, in a lateral direction, thereby prolonging their residence time in the molten pool. In laser welding, the action of recoil pressure is opposite to the direction of gas escape. Combined with increased melt viscosity compared to GTAW and other arc welding processes, this results in higher porosity sensitivity. In GMA welding, droplet impact may bring gas deep into the molten pool. In addition, heat input affects the formation of pores by changing the geometry of the molten pool and the state of oxide particles. In engineering applications, the mechanical properties and reliability of weldments will be significantly reduced if there are porosity defects in welds. Therefore, it is also a challenge for ODS superalloys to effectively suppress the porosity defects in the welding process of ODS superalloys, and the method of combining material characteristics with process parameter optimization is the focus of future welding research.

sections.heading: Degradation of long-term service behaviors
paragraphs: For ODS superalloys, both fusion welding and solid-state welding can achieve alloy connection. However, due to the higher welding temperature, the research focus of fusion welding is more on controlling the evolution of oxide particles during the welding process, rather than controlling residual stress. Therefore, this section will focus on the residual stress formation mechanism, distribution, and the impact of welding on the long-term service performance of ODS superalloys under FSW.

Compared with traditional alloys, ODS superalloys strengthened by oxide particles typically have extremely high yield strength. Welding residual stress often exceeds the yield strength of the material [ 53 ], leading to worsening stress concentration at the weld and becoming a key factor in crack formation [ 54 ]. The high yield strength of ODS superalloys indicates their stronger ability to withstand thermal stress without yielding. When combined with the pinning of grain boundaries and dislocations by oxide particles, these alloys cannot release stress like typical alloys, resulting in an increase in welding residual stress. The combination of a large amount of residual stress and poor creep ductility in ODS superalloys often leads to cracking at weakened grain boundaries during subsequent heating processes [ 55 ]. Dawson et al. [ 56 ] found significant residual stresses in all FSW ODS alloy joints, with longitudinal stresses being higher than transverse stresses (as shown in Fig.  14 ). The tensile stress level in the thermomechanical influence zone (TMAZ) mainly depends on the post-weld cooling rate. Therefore, although reducing lateral velocity can alleviate these stresses, the resulting high-temperature thermal cycles may endanger the stability of oxide particles. Brewer et al. [ 57 ] characterized the FSW MA956 ODS steel weld using X-ray and neutron diffraction and also found the phenomenon of significant residual stress in the plate (as shown in Fig.  15 ). The longitudinal residual stress of the weld seam is much greater than the transverse stress, and the root stress is higher than the crown stress. The residual stress in the TMAZ area is as high as 80% of the strength of the base material, and the residual stress in the center of the mixing zone also reaches 40–50% of the yield strength of the material. Fig. 14 a – c  Transverse weld residual stress cloud maps,  d – f  Longitudinal weld residual stress cloud maps,  g  Longitudinal and  h  Transverse line scan residual stress data at 1.4 mm from the weld top surface,  i  Peak tensile residual stress,  j  Peak temperature and cooling rate as a function of transverse speed during welding. Reprinted from [ 56 ] with permission. Copyright 2017 Elsevier Fig. 15 Residual stress distributions measured by neutron diffraction: blue line and symbols 500/25, green line and symbols 400/50, red line and symbols 400/100;  a  Longitudinal residual stress,  b  Transverse residual stress,  c  Normal stress. Reprinted from [ 57 ] with permission. Copyright 2015 Elsevier

The above results indicate that residual stresses generated during FSW of ODS superalloys are significant and difficult to avoid. Therefore, it is necessary to have a deeper understanding of the impact of residual stresses on the long-term service behavior of welded components. However, research experiments on the service behavior of ODS superalloy welded parts are currently very limited. For fatigue performance, this section will cite the study of fatigue performance of ODS superalloy welded with dissimilar metals as auxiliary evidence. Yamazaki et al. [ 58 ] conducted high-temperature fatigue tests on the diffusion-bonded joints of ODS superalloy MA758 and superalloys CM-247LC and plotted the S–N curve at 950 ℃. As shown in Fig.  16 , the fatigue strength of the dissimilar joint is slightly lower than that of the ODS base material. Based on the approximate curve obtained by the least squares method, the stress of the ODS superalloy base material is about 160 MPa at 107 cycles, while the stress of the dissimilar joint is about 147 MPa, and the fatigue strength decreases by about 20%. For creep performance, Wang et al. [ 59 ] conducted creep experiments on friction stir welded MA754 ODS superalloy. The results showed that the creep resistance of the weld seam was significantly reduced compared to the base metal. Power law creep behavior was observed at 973 K and 1073 K, with stress indices of 6.9 and 6.3, respectively. And through 1-h 1598 K post-weld heat treatment, the grain structure can be coarsened, effectively suppressing the degradation of creep performance. The result is shown in Fig.  17 . Fig. 16 S–N curveof the joints tested at 950 °C. Reprinted from [ 58 ] with permission. Copyright 2001 The Society of  Materials Science, Japan Fig. 17 a  Strain–time curves for AR, FSW, and ANN-FSW materials tested at 1073 K.  b  The variation of creep rate with applied stress for AR, FSW, and FSW-ANN materials. Reprinted from [ 59 ] with permission. Copyright 2014 Springer Nature

Overall, ODS superalloys tend to retain a significant residual stress tendency after welding, with longitudinal stress being the dominant force. The combined effect of residual stress and microstructure evolution caused by welding has a significant impact on the long-term service performance of welded joints. It can lead to a decrease in fatigue strength and creep resistance, making it a challenge for welding ODS superalloys.

sections.heading: Techniques for increasing ODS superalloys' weldability
Welding process parameters
paragraphs: The most common method for welding ODS superalloys is friction stir welding, and there hasn't been much research done on fusion welding. Wang et al. [ 59 ] summarized that using the process parameters Tool rotation rate of 1000 rpm and Traverse speed of 50.8 mm/min, defect free welds can be obtained after MA754 friction stir welding. In order to assess appropriate FSW process parameters, Baker et al. [ 60 ] defined the pseudo-heat index (RPM/IPM), which is the ratio of tool rotational speed to tool translational speed. To produce totally fused, defect-free welds, the minimum pseudo-heat index range should be between 100 and 150. The mechanical characteristics of the welded joint were better when the friction pressure was 50 MPa, 70 MPa, and 100 MPa, according to research by Ates et al. [ 61 ] on the impact of friction pressure on FSW welding of MA956. However, the mechanical characteristics significantly decreased when the friction pressure reached 40 MPa because it was not high enough to provide the heat needed for friction welding. As seen in Fig.  18 , A good connection can be achieved when the friction time is 6 s. Wang et al. [ 62 ] studied the joint quality of PM2000 at a welding speed of 1–3 mm/s in friction stir welding and found that there were only a few gaps at the interface between SZ and RS-TMAZ at 2 mm/s. By adjusting the welding process window, when the welding speed is 3 mm/s, the strength, ductility, and toughness of the welded joint are optimal (as shown in Table  1 ). The impact of various process factors on the material's mechanical properties must also be taken into account once defect-free welds have been achieved. When FSW 4 mm thick MA956 under various process conditions, Brewer et al. [ 57 ] discovered that oxide particles showed varied degrees of coarsening. In the base material, the oxide particle size was 8.1 nm, 166 nm at 400 rpm/100 mmpm, and 343 nm at 500 rpm/25 mmpm. In the meantime, the longitudinal residual stress will lower the fatigue strength of the ODS superalloy plate because the amount of residual stress in the weld is inversely proportional to the ratio of rotational speed to translational speed during welding. The connection welded at a rotational speed of 250 rpm had a maximum tensile strength of 974 MPa, or roughly 84% of the base material (as shown in Fig.  19 ), according to Han et al.'s study [ 63 ] on the impact of various rotational speeds on FSW joints. But the excessive rotation speed raises the temperature and reduces the material's tensile strength because of the coarsening of the grains brought on by continuing dynamic recrystallization. Yabuuchi et al. [ 64 ] experimentally showed that the coarsening of recrystallized grains during FSW affects the tensile strength and hardness of ODS steel, while the tool rotation speed has a negligible effect on the change in the size of oxide particles. When Zhao et al. [ 65 ] studied the FSW ODS-Cu and T91 tube-to-tube connections, no defects were discovered at the joints; however, EDS testing indicated asymmetric element diffusion. Even when the welded sections were annealed at various temperatures, tensile brittleness occurred. According to the research, the soft zone identified by microhardness testing is linked to the brittle behavior rather than quenched martensite. In order to solve the tensile brittle fracture challenge, additional process parameter optimization is necessary. Fig. 19 Tensile properties at room temperature:  a  Stress–strain curves;  b  Ultimate tensile strength (UTS) and total elongation. Reprinted from [ 63 ] with permission. Copyright 2018 Elsevier

Some researchers have successfully produced well-formed, less defective joints by attempting fusion welding of ODS superalloys. Lemmen et al. [ 66 ] successfully applied laser welding to ODS superalloy PM1000, and the results showed that the optimal weld quality was achieved when the heat input was 24–36 J/mm and the scanning rate was 100 mm/s. The proposed weld morphology (related to heat input) has a strong influence on the failure behavior of ODS superalloy at high temperatures. But when the scanning rate exceeds 80 mm/s, porosity and other phenomena may occur at the weld seam (as shown in Fig.  20 ). Fu et al. [ 48 ] studied the effect of pulse laser welding parameters on the quality of ODS Eurofer steel welds using a 2500 W laser power and 2–5 ms pulse time. When the pulse time is less than 2.5 ms, partial penetration occurs, and there are large pores at the bottom of the weld seam. When the pulse time is longer than 2.5 ms, a small number of micropores can be observed under the light microscope. Therefore, the process parameters of fusion welding need to be regulated in three aspects: penetration, porosity control, and material loss. Zhang et al. [ 67 ] prepared FeCrAl ODS superalloy using laser selective melting technology (SLM) and designed the effects of different process parameters on the morphology and internal defects of the welded parts through orthogonal experiments. The process parameters include laser power of 300–320 W, scanning speed of 650–850 mm/s, and scanning spacing of 0.05–0.07 mm. The metallographic results are shown in Fig.  21 , and the porosity is marked in the lower left corner of the image. According to the results of the orthogonal experiment, it can be seen that the process parameters have a significant impact on the porosity of the weld seam, with porosity concentrated between 0.5% and 4.5%. When the scanning spacing is 0.05 mm and 0.07 mm, a large number of pores and crack defects are generated. When the scanning spacing is too large and the overlap between adjacent weld beads is insufficient; When the scanning spacing is too small, the sensitivity of the weld seam to thermal cracking increases. When the scanning spacing is 0.06 mm, the porosity defect is improved compared to the other two conditions. The optimal process parameters are a laser power of 310 W, a scanning speed of 650 mm/s, and a scanning spacing of 0.06 mm, with a porosity of only 0.5%. In a comparison of TIG and laser welding seams, Molian et al. [ 68 ] discovered that both welding techniques result in a reduction in joint hardness. Hardness decreases in laser-welded parts due to the loss of grain orientation. Oxide agglomeration and loss of grain orientation work together to reduce hardness in TIG-welded parts (as shown in Fig.  22 ). Zhu et al. [ 41 ] discovered that the tensile strength of ODS steel was only 410 MPa after TIG welding. The tensile strength could be raised to 550 MPa when arc ultrasonic support was introduced and the excitation current reached 20–30 A; however, the weld hardness was not much improved by this technique. This section summarizes the influence of ODS superalloy welding process parameters on weld quality and mechanical properties. The research on FSW of ODS superalloy is relatively mature. By optimizing parameters such as welding speed, rotational speed, and friction pressure, defect-free welds can be obtained and the mechanical properties of the joint can be improved. However, research on melting welding of ODS superalloy is relatively lacking. The process window of laser welding and pulse laser welding needs to balance three factors: penetration, porosity control, and material loss among parameters such as heat input, scanning speed, and pulse time. In selective laser melting technology, optimizing the scanning spacing is particularly crucial for controlling porosity and crack defects. For TIG welding, introducing auxiliary means can improve the joint performance to a certain extent. In summary, by finely adjusting the process parameters, high-quality ODS superalloy welded joints can be obtained in different welding methods.

sections.heading: Composition design
paragraphs: In addition to adjusting process parameters, the composition design of ODS superalloys is an essential technique for preventing welding difficulties throughout the welding process. Compared to other alloys, ODS superalloys have the distinct advantage of improving welding mechanical properties through the synergistic effect of matrix alloy composition and internal oxide strengthening particles. Among these, utilizing filler materials for welding is a popular component design strategy.

Liang et al. [ 69 ] investigated the differences between laser-welded ODS superalloy joints with and without filler powder. The base metal was Fe-0.18C-19.34Cr-5.06Al-0.5Ti-0.017N-0.26O-0.51Y 2 O 3 , while the filler powder was Fe-0.25C-2.00Y 2 O 3 -23.00Cr-30Ni-1.0Ti-0.35Si-0.4Al. The addition of filler powder generated two types of high-melting-point and uniformly distributed oxide particles in the weld metal, simultaneously improving the tensile strength and hardness of the welded joint (as shown in Fig.  23 ), demonstrating the feasibility of using filler powder laser welding for ODS superalloys. Kazempour-Liasi et al. [ 70 ] improved the weldability of superalloy IN939 by using five solid solution alloys (HAYNES 230, IN625, IN617, HASTELLOY X, HAYNES 25) and two precipitation-strengthened alloys (IN718, HAYNES C-263) as filler metals in TIG welding. The results demonstrated that when the filler metal's Al + Ti + Nb + Ta + Mo + W content was lower than that of the base metal, cracking during post-weld heat treatment could be successfully minimized. The impact of nickel-based superalloys 609 and 709 as filler metals on the microstructure and mechanical characteristics of 9% nickel steel was compared by Hwang et al. [ 71 ]. It was discovered that alloy 709 may suppress the production of martensite while reducing the ρ-phase precipitates in the dendritic region and producing a thicker γ-stabilized layer (Ni, Cr, Mo, and Mn) at the weld. And the superalloy 709 weld showed finer particles and a reduced CGHAZ volume fraction. Because of these experimental results, the weld's hardness and impact toughness increased, suggesting that superalloy 709 was a better filler metal for the base metal than 609. Reprinted from [ 69 ] with permission. Copyright  2015 Elsevier

The composition and proportion of the matrix, oxide dispersoids, and filler materials can be modified to solve the performance deterioration and cracking issues that arise during the welding of ODS superalloys. High-temperature strength and welding process adaptability should be thoroughly taken into account while designing the matrix alloy. For example, the formation of brittle metallic phases can be avoided by balancing the effects of precipitation strengthening with the grain boundary stability of the heat-affected zone by varying the content of γ phase-forming elements and microalloying elements (such as boron, silicon, and phosphorus). To prevent particle agglomeration and guarantee their uniform dispersion throughout the microstructure, the content of oxide dispersoids (such as Y 2 O 3 ) can be modified. Filler materials should be designed with the weld metal in mind, providing appropriate grain boundary strengthening components and minimizing alloy components that are prone to solidification cracking. This technique may improve the overall performance of the welded joint, enhance the high-temperature mechanical properties of the weld zone, and effectively inhibit the tendency of solidification fractures in the weld metal.

sections.heading: Post-weld treatment
paragraphs: Post-weld treatment is an important stage in the welding process because it can improve the microstructure and characteristics of the joint and successfully remove residual stresses brought on by the welding process. The addition of oxide particles is what gives ODS superalloys their superior mechanical properties. Nevertheless, at high temperatures, these oxide particles are not very stable [ 72 ]. Conventional post-weld heat treatment (PWHT) techniques are challenging to remove post-weld stress and may reduce their strengthening impact [ 73 ]. In order to enhance joint performance and guarantee that the joint satisfies the demands of extreme service environments, it is crucial to carry out focused research on post-weld treatment for ODS superalloys.

Fu et al. [ 74 ] studied the post-weld heat treatment of dissimilar FSW joints between 9Cr ODS and CLF-1 steel and found that as the PWHT temperature increased, the width and grain size of the recrystallized equiaxed zone in the CLF-1 side weld increased, but recrystallization did not reduce the joint connection performance. Post-weld treatment can transform the original quenched martensite in the weld into tempered martensite with higher strength. Figure  24 f also shows the main types of oxide particles present. The study by Manugula et al. [ 75 ] showed that the impact toughness of joints welded at low speeds of 200 rpm was close to that of the base metal in the as-welded state, while the impact toughness of joints welded at high speeds of 700 rpm was poor. Post-weld heat treatment can significantly reduce the hardness of the weld zone, but different heat treatment methods have different effects: direct post-weld tempering (PWDT) causes coarsening and merging of precipitated phases in the heat-affected zone, resulting in uneven distribution of joint hardness; And post-weld normalizing and tempering (PWNT) can precipitate particles with microstructure characteristics similar to the original state of the base metal at grain boundaries and subgrain boundaries. Therefore, the best combination of microstructure and mechanical properties can be obtained by using PWNT treatment at a low speed of 200 rpm. The strengthening effect of post-weld heat treatment on ODS superalloy joints is also reflected in other material systems. Tao et al. [ 76 ] studied the welding joint of ODS AA6063 aluminum-based composite material after PWHT and found that the microhardness value in the stirring zone significantly increased after post-weld heat treatment, which was attributed to the contributions of AlFeSi intermetallic compounds, Al oxide particles, and β'' precipitates (as shown in Fig.  25 ). The bonding efficiency of ultimate tensile strength reached 92%. The results indicate that regulating precipitation behavior and particle distribution through PWHT is an effective way to improve the performance of FSW joints in ODS materials, providing useful references for post-weld heat treatment research of ODS superalloys. As mentioned earlier, there is a contradiction between residual stress relief and tissue retention in post-weld heat treatment of ODS superalloys. This contradiction can be resolved through the following potential paths. Local heat treatment techniques (such as primary heating + secondary heating [ 77 ] and strategies such as reducing heating rate [ 78 ]) can achieve precise heat input to the weld zone and achieve ideal stress states in critical areas. The cooling rate of post-weld aging treatment has a significant impact on the performance of welded joints. Reducing the cooling rate can increase the proportion of special grain boundaries in the heat-affected zone, thereby suppressing crack propagation and improving creep performance [ 79 ]. This discovery indicates that in the design of post-weld heat treatment processes for ODS alloys, in addition to temperature and holding time, cooling rate is also a parameter that needs to be considered. Vibration aging technology can also provide an efficient and low-cost alternative solution for eliminating residual stresses after welding. Research has shown that vibration treatment after welding can significantly reduce the residual stress of the material [ 80 ]. This technology does not require high temperatures and can fundamentally avoid the risk of oxide particle agglomeration and dissolution during post-weld heat treatment of ODS superalloy.

sections.heading: Conclusions
paragraphs: This article reviews the main challenges and coping strategies of ODS superalloys in the welding process. And organize, compare, and analyze existing literature from the aspects of process parameter optimization, composition design, and post-weld treatment. The main conclusions obtained are as follows: The main strengthening methods of ODS superalloys are the synergistic effect of dispersion strengthening and grain refinement strengthening. The main challenges faced by its welding include agglomeration and decomposition of oxides, porosity defects, and degradation of long-term service behavior. The root cause lies in the contradiction between the instability of oxide particles and welding thermal cycles. The welding method of ODS superalloys needs to be selected according to actual needs. Melting welding has high efficiency and mature technology, but the high temperature of the melt pool inevitably leads to the evolution of oxide particles. Solid-phase welding has a lower temperature, which can better preserve oxide particles, but it will introduce larger residual stresses. Subsequent research needs to simultaneously consider the retention of oxide particles, residual stress control, and defect elimination. Process parameter optimization, composition design, and post-weld treatment are three methods that can improve the mechanical properties of ODS superalloy welds, but each method has its own limitations. Optimization of process parameters can only alleviate problems within a limited range and is difficult to fundamentally solve; although adjusting the composition can improve the thermal stability of particles, it usually comes at the cost of sacrificing other properties; post-weld treatment faces the fundamental contradiction between stress relief and particle stability. The existing research on welding of ODS superalloys is usually limited to one material, lacking a comparison of welding of multiple materials and extraction of universal rules. The comparability between different studies is poor, resulting in each study being relatively independent.

ODS superalloys have superior performance and great potential in practical applications. Based on the above conclusion, future research can seek breakthroughs from the following aspects. A novel ODS welding wire can be developed to facilitate the in-situ synthesis of oxide particles during the welding process, thereby compensating for the loss of oxide particles in the weld zone induced by welding. Through synergistic design of alloy composition and welding parameters, the weldability of ODS superalloys can be fundamentally enhanced. Through the application of in-situ characterization techniques, transient phenomena during the welding process, including the evolution of oxide particles, dislocation dynamics, grain boundary migration, and defect formation, can be elucidated. For instance, in-situ transmission electron microscopy coupled with microcalorimetry enables the investigation of oxide particle coarsening mechanisms under thermal cycling, while synchrotron X-ray imaging facilitates the real-time tracking of pore evolution. These advanced methodologies offer the potential to visualize dynamic changes during welding, thereby enabling predictive insights into oxide and microstructural evolution and providing guidance for process optimization. ODS superalloys have special characteristics. Research should focus on how the microstructure and properties of their welded joints change under high temperature, strong irradiation, and high pressure. Based on this, a full life cycle performance database and life prediction model can be established. Artificial intelligence can be introduced to assist in optimizing process parameters. By analyzing existing data, the relationship between process parameters, microstructure, and mechanical properties can be identified. This approach enables the rapid determination of optimal process parameters.
